Glutinous means sticky, thick, and glue-like in texture — the kind of stickiness where something clings to your fingers, stretches when you pull it, and resists coming off cleanly. Think of honey dripping slowly from a spoon, or the way cooked oatmeal sticks to a bowl. That quality — that thick, clinging, adhesive consistency — is what "glutinous" captures.

If something is glutinous, it behaves a lot like glue: it sticks, it's gooey, it pulls and clings.
What It Feels and Looks Like

To really feel the word, picture these sensations:

  • You touch something and it grabs your finger slightly.
  • When you pull your finger away, the substance either stretches or leaves a sticky trace.
  • It's not just wet — it's clingingly wet, with a thickness and body to it.
  • It pours slowly, not freely.

That combination of thickness + stickiness + clinginess is the heart of "glutinous."

1. Food — most commonly
This is by far the most frequent use. Foods can be glutinous when cooked or processed in a way that makes them sticky and dense.

  • Glutinous rice (also called sticky rice) is a famous example — when cooked, the grains stick together in a clumpy, gluey mass rather than staying separate and fluffy like regular rice. It's widely used in Asian cuisines.
  • Overcooked pasta can become glutinous — thick, gummy, and sticking to itself.
  • Certain puddings, porridges, and dumplings are described as glutinous because of their dense, sticky texture.
  • Melted marshmallows, caramel sauce, or thick syrup are all glutinous.

2. Natural substances

  • Wet clay and mud after heavy rain can be glutinous — heavy, sticky, sucking at your boots.
  • Tree sap or resin is often glutinous — thick, slow, and clingy.
  • Some insects produce glutinous secretions to trap prey.

3. Any sticky, viscous material in general
A scientist might describe a lab substance as glutinous. A chef might warn that a sauce has become glutinous. A writer might describe a swamp as having glutinous mud. The word fits anywhere the idea of thick, clinging stickiness applies.

Glutinous sits in the moderate-to-high range of stickiness. It's not the light, surface-level tackiness of a Post-it note. It's a heavier, more enveloping stickiness — the kind that slows things down and makes them cling together. But it's not necessarily as rigid or bonding as actual glue. Think of it as behaving like glue rather than being glue.

These words overlap with glutinous but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Sticky — the broadest, most everyday word. Glutinous is a more specific and formal version of sticky, emphasizing thickness and a glue-like quality.
  • Viscous — refers mainly to how slowly a liquid flows (like thick syrup or oil). Glutinous adds the element of stickiness on top of that thickness.
  • Gluey — almost a synonym, informal. Glutinous is the more refined word.
  • Gooey — informal, often used affectionately (gooey chocolate cake). Glutinous is more neutral or clinical.
  • Gelatinous — jelly-like and wobbly (like Jell-O). Gelatinous things jiggle; glutinous things stick. They can overlap, but they're not the same.
  • Mucilaginous — sticky and slimy like mucus (okra is a good example). More biological/organic in feel.
A Very Common Mistake to Avoid

Because the word looks similar to "gluten", many people assume that glutinous means containing gluten (the protein found in wheat). This is incorrect.

Glutinous refers purely to a texture — the sticky, gluey quality. It says nothing about the presence or absence of the protein gluten. In fact, glutinous rice is typically considered gluten-free, even though its very name has "glut-" in it. The name comes from its glue-like, sticky texture — not from gluten the protein. This is one of the most important things to know about this word.

• "The porridge had been left on the stove too long and had turned glutinous and thick."
  • "She pulled her boot out of the glutinous mud with a loud sucking sound."
  • "The dumplings were made with glutinous rice flour, giving them their famously chewy, sticky skin."
  • "The syrup reduced until it became a glutinous, dark caramel that coated the back of the spoon."
  • "The wound was sealed with a glutinous substance secreted by the insect."
Glutinous means having the thick, sticky, clinging quality of glue — used to describe foods, substances, or materials that stick together, adhere to surfaces, and resist flowing or separating freely.
